Clinical Vignette: Sarah

Sarah is a 38-year-old bartender who has worked at the same upscale cocktail bar in the city for the past twelve years. She's known for her precision-the way she can execute a dozen drink orders without writing anything down, how she remembers regulars' preferences, how she manages the rhythm of a busy Friday night with an almost meditative calm. Her partner of eight years, Marcus, used to joke that she was wasted on bartending; he'd say she could manage anything. That was before.

Three years ago, Marcus was hit by a car while crossing the street after work. Sarah wasn't there. She was behind the bar, doing what she does, when the police called. The impact fractured his femur in three places and caused a traumatic brain injury. He spent six weeks in the hospital. He recovered physically, mostly, though he walks with a slight limp now and tires easily. But the man who came home wasn't quite Marcus anymore.

Sarah stopped working for two months after the accident. When she returned to the bar, everything felt different. The noise-which had always energized her, the clink of glasses and murmur of conversation-now made her chest tight. She'd find herself gripping the edge of the bar, her jaw clenched, unable to focus on the drink orders. Loud sounds, particularly anything sharp or sudden, would send her heart racing. A glass breaking would make her flinch so violently that her coworkers started asking if she was okay.

The nights are worse. Sarah lies awake next to Marcus, her mind cycling through the what-ifs. What if he'd left work five minutes earlier? What if she'd picked him up that day? What if the driver had been paying attention? She can't stop imagining the moment of impact, even though she wasn't there to see it. Sometimes she wakes gasping, convinced she's heard the sound of the collision-a sound she's never actually heard but has constructed in her mind so vividly it feels like a memory.

During the day, Sarah moves through the bar mechanically. She's still competent; the drinks are still perfect. But she no longer anticipates the rush or feels that sense of flow she once loved. Instead, she's hypervigilant in a way that exhausts her. She notices every person who walks through the door. She tracks exits. She's acutely aware of anything that could go wrong. When a customer gets rowdy, she doesn't feel her usual confidence in de-escalation; instead, she feels trapped, her body flooded with adrenaline.

At home, she's withdrawn from Marcus in ways she doesn't fully understand. He's trying-he's always trying-but sometimes when she looks at him, she sees not the person she loves but a reminder of that day, of how fragile everything is, of how quickly everything can change. She snaps at him over small things. She avoids intimacy. Part of her knows this isn't his fault, but another part of her resents him for surviving, for being hurt, for making her feel this way.

Sarah drinks more than she used to, even though she's surrounded by alcohol all day. A glass of wine at home helps quiet the intrusive thoughts, at least temporarily. She's stopped seeing friends. She's stopped doing the things she used to enjoy. Her world has become smaller, constricted, a careful navigation around the edges of her fear. She knows something is wrong with her, but naming it feels like giving up.
